title: Linear dynamic versus constant online locality for a promise-free LCL
formal: Does there exist one promise-free LCL on bounded-degree graphs with deterministic online-LOCAL complexity O(1), but deterministic incremental dynamic-LOCAL complexity Ω(n)? Under the models below, the answer is no: constant online locality implies deterministic O(√n·polylog n) LOCAL complexity and hence a sublinear dynamic repair radius.
definitions: A promise-free LCL Π has one fixed degree bound Δ≥2, one fixed checking radius r≥1, finite vertex input/output alphabets, and a finite list of permitted rooted radius-r input/output neighborhoods. A labeling is legal exactly when all vertices pass this check. The problem must admit a legal output for every finite simple undirected graph of degree at most Δ and every input assignment, including disconnected graphs. Legality is invariant under isomorphism and does not depend on identifiers, port orders, or graph size. No assumption of bipartiteness, planarity, a rooted structure, or a special global input encoding is made. In deterministic online-LOCAL, the eventual graph has n vertices, n is known, and an adversary requests every vertex once in an arbitrary order. At the request for v, the entire radius-R(n) neighborhood of v in the eventual graph is revealed, including input labels and edges in the accumulated revealed subgraph. The algorithm has global memory, but must choose v’s final output immediately and never change a previous output. All final outputs must be legal for every graph and request order. It has no advance access to the rest of the eventual graph. In incremental dynamic-LOCAL, a central deterministic algorithm starts with the empty graph and a known upper bound N on the eventual number of vertices. An adversary inserts isolated vertices with immutable input labels and identifiers, or inserts edges between existing vertices, always respecting Δ and the size bound. After every event the algorithm must maintain a legal output on the entire current graph. Existing outputs may change only within distance R(N) of an endpoint of the inserted edge, or of the inserted vertex, measured after the event. The algorithm may inspect the entire revealed graph and retain arbitrary state, but future vertices, inputs, and edges are unknown. The locality is the largest radius of any output change, not the number of changes or the update time. All algorithms are uniform finite programs, all local computation must terminate, and all guarantees are deterministic and worst case. A constant locality bound is independent of size and may depend only on the fixed problem. A linear lower bound means that for every correct algorithm A there are a constant c_A>0 and arbitrarily large size bounds with an input or update sequence forcing locality at least c_A times that bound. This infinitely-often formulation is already ruled out by a uniform sublinear upper bound.
answer_criterion: A positive answer requires one finite total LCL specification, a constant-locality online algorithm, and a linear dynamic-radius lower bound for all deterministic maintenance algorithms. A negative answer excludes every such witness. The cited simulations imply the negative answer; the conclusion is an editorial composition of the results, with its reasoning given below.
context:
Online lookaround reveals nearby parts of the eventual graph before a vertex commits to its output. Incremental dynamic computation instead sees the graph as it is built and repairs earlier outputs. The question asks whether even constant lookaround can prevent changes that would otherwise have to spread linearly far.

These are spatial resource bounds. A dynamic algorithm may examine the whole current graph and perform very expensive computation, yet its output changes must remain close to the update. An online algorithm may use all previously revealed information but cannot revise a requested vertex. Neither definition bounds ordinary centralized running time.

The first step removes dependence on unrelated revealed components. Lemma 7.5 turns an online algorithm of locality T(n) into one whose decision depends only on its current revealed component, with locality T(2^O(n³)). If T is a constant, this enormous change of the size argument leaves locality constant. The family of all bounded-degree graphs satisfies the lemma’s closure assumptions.

The second step simulates that component-wise algorithm in sublinear deterministic LOCAL time. The clustering framework separates small-diameter regions with only O(√n) leftover vertices. Grouping nearby leftovers gives components of diameter O(√n) whose constant-radius views are mutually separate. Each such component can simulate the deterministic online rule on its leftovers independently; these simulations form one valid online prefix. Each remaining region can then choose a compatible completion by finite exhaustive search. Local checkability makes the separate completions compatible. The total communication radius is O(√n·polylog n). This explains the deterministic specialization of the component-wise simulation.

A deterministic T(n)-round LOCAL algorithm also supplies a dynamic algorithm with repair radius at most T(n)+O(1). Recompute its prescribed outputs after each insertion. Farther vertices have unchanged input neighborhoods and therefore unchanged outputs. For growing graphs, use the fixed size bound N and pad unseen vertices as isolated vertices with fixed dummy inputs; the problem is total and its legality is independent of N, so outputs on the real components remain valid.

The complete implication is online O(1) → component-wise online O(1) → deterministic LOCAL O(√n·polylog n) → dynamic O(√n·polylog n). This excludes the requested linear dynamic lower bound. It does not prove that online and dynamic locality always agree, nor give a constant-radius dynamic simulation.
why: This asks whether a small view into the eventual graph can eliminate a global repair cost. Its negative resolution is a useful constraint on future separation constructions: a promise-free LCL with constant online locality must already permit sublinear dynamic repair.

importance.reason: A structural comparison of online lookaround and dynamic repair, now bounded by a general sublinear simulation. Preserved as a resolved historical question, distinct from the separate LOCAL-versus-dynamic comparison.

progress.text: Akbari and coauthors formalize online lookaround and incremental dynamic locality and establish LOCAL → dynamic-LOCAL → online-LOCAL simulations.

The primary problem list records the promise-free linear-versus-constant separation target. Lemma 7.5 of the corrected comparison paper turns constant online locality into constant component-wise online locality on all bounded-degree graphs.

The general-graph clustering simulation yields a sublinear deterministic LOCAL algorithm from a constant-locality component-wise online algorithm. The revised paper explains the online extension in Section 1.6 and Appendix A.

Combine that sublinear LOCAL algorithm with local recomputation after updates. The resulting O(√n·polylog n) repair radius contradicts any linear dynamic lower bound, so the saved separation target has a negative answer.

status_note: Resolved negatively in the specified promise-free deterministic models by composition of the cited simulations. The derivation is made explicit rather than attributed to an exact theorem statement about this catalogue ID. The conclusion concerns linear-versus-constant separation, not equivalence of the two models.
